item.description:
Government, semi-government, autonomous, semi-autonomous and private offices will reopen tomorrow, Sunday, after a five-day Durga Puja holiday. Banks and courts will also resume operations.

A holiday had been declared from 20 to 22 October for Durga Puja this year. According to the government holiday calendar, 20 October, Tuesday, had already been declared a holiday by executive order on the occasion of Maha Navami.

Puja holidays: Tk 5m, 8 bhori of gold missing from home

The following day, 21 October, Wednesday, was a general holiday for Bijoya Dashami. Later, 22 October, Thursday, was also declared a holiday by executive order, bringing the Durga Puja holiday period to three days, from 20 to 22 October.

Friday and Saturday, 23 and 24 October, were the weekly holidays. As a result, the five-day break continued through today, Saturday. However, offices had remained open on the preceding Saturday, 17 October, before the holiday period began.

item.title: 5 Bangladeshis charged in Canadian immigration fraud case, 1 faces arrest warrant
item.description:
Five Bangladeshis have been charged with three offences in an immigration fraud case in Canada following an investigation by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).

The CBSA disclosed the information in a press release published on the Canadian government’s website on Thursday.

Four of the accused — Rashel Mirza, Mohammad Aminul Islam, Md Mudassar Alam Bhuiyan and Kazi Nafiz Alam — appeared at a court in Valleyfield, Quebec, on 22 October.

The fifth accused, Md Rakibul Hasan, is reportedly in Bangladesh. An arrest warrant has been issued for him.

Italy, Greece, and Cyprus send back 35 Bangladeshis

According to the CBSA press release, the agency conducted a raid on a building in Mercier, Quebec, on 3 July 2024. Officers and representatives from the Mercier police and fire services were also present.

After the raid uncovered several indications of violations of Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the CBSA began investigating the activities of the accused in August that year.

The investigation found that a total of 243 temporary resident visa (TRV) applications had been submitted on behalf of 209 Bangladeshi nationals.

The applications stated that the applicants intended to visit Canada at the invitation of Canadian citizens. However, investigators allege that forged documents and false information were used in the applications to obtain visas.

Canada Express Entry: Up to 100 extra points for high-wage jobs, key changes announced
Given the scale and complexity of the fraud, investigators focused on 79 visa applications for which they had found the most serious evidence. Three charges have been brought against the accused.

Investigators said a group had been operating in a coordinated and planned manner to help Bangladeshis obtain visas by using forged documents and false information.

On 3 June 2025, CBSA investigators searched four locations in Quebec and Ontario. Documents, computer equipment and other evidence recovered during the searches indicated that the five individuals were involved in visa fraud.

Given the scale and complexity of the fraud, investigators focused on 79 visa applications for which they had found the most serious evidence.

Three charges have been brought against the accused. The first is conspiring to help one or more people enter Canada illegally.

The second is knowingly helping to conceal crucial information or provide false information in visa applications. The third is knowingly encouraging or assisting others to violate Canadian immigration law.

New rules for studying in Canada: Tighter scrutiny of study permits

However, the charges are still awaiting scrutiny by the court.

Canada’s Minister of Public Safety, Gary Anandasangaree, said the country’s immigration system operated on the principles of integrity, fairness and respect for the law.

Anyone who sought to exploit the system through fraud or undermine its reputation would face serious consequences, he said. He thanked CBSA staff for their work to protect border security and uphold the integrity of the immigration system.

Eric Lapierre, the CBSA’s regional director general for Quebec, said the agency was working to identify and stop groups that abused Canada’s immigration system.

He described the investigation as part of that effort and praised the agency’s criminal investigators for their work in maintaining public confidence in immigration programmes.

item.title: Artist Kamrul Hasan Lipu explores his roots in Yokohama solo exhibition
item.description:
Despite his many years in Japan, artist Kamrul Hasan Lipu continues to return to the people, nature and folk traditions of Bangladesh in his paintings.

Women's faces, water lilies, sari ornamentation and arrangements of red and green reflect his continuing relationship with his birthplace.

These concerns and different stages of his practice come together in his first solo exhibition, “DOT: The Beginning of Everything”, at Gallery Shimizu in Yokohama. Its Bengali subtitle is “Bindu Theke Srishty.”

The exhibition opened at 3:00 pm on 20 October, with Matsudo City Councillor Mir Kazue attending as chief guest.

Other guests included Japanese painter Asano Yasunori, an adviser to the Yokohama Port Independent Exhibition; paper-cutting artist Mita Chikako; and Gallery Shimizu representative Kazue Shimizu.

Featuring 41 artworks, the exhibition runs until 25 October.

Art exhibition: Where past, present and future converge

The title offers an entry point into the artist's understanding of creation: a dot becomes a line, a line develops into a form, and forms give shape to the visible world.

Artist Kamrul Hasan Lipu connects this idea with his own journey, bringing together childhood drawing, years of practice and experiences of life in Bangladesh and Japan.

Women's faces are a central subject in his visual language. The folds of a sari, jewellery, flowers in the hair and facial expressions evoke familiar aspects of Bengali life.

Alongside beauty, these works suggest sensitivity, dignity and emotional strength. Direct gazes, quiet expressions and contemplative figures invite viewers to consider an inner world.

Works including “The Bede Girl”, “Madhabi”, “Mrinalini” and “Beyond the Blue” explore different aspects of this subject. In “The Sari of Stories”, arrangements of a woman, a peacock, birds and flowers turn the sari into a bearer of memory and narrative. Folk ornamentation and the vibrant visual traditions of rickshaw painting also inform his compositions.

Water lilies carry a personal childhood memory for Lipu. At the age of eight, he began drawing them for an art competition with only three coloured pencils. He later borrowed pencils from others to add more colours and won third prize.

Recounted in his catalogue statement, this experience gives a personal dimension to the exhibition's theme. For him, the water lily recalls the beginning of his artistic journey as well as the natural world.

In works such as “Exuberance of Water Lilies” and “Awaiting Bloom”, flowers, buds and colour suggest life and possibility.

“Childhood Beyond the Kite String” recalls the rooftops and kites of Old Dhaka, while the red and green in “The Flag of Independence” connect personal experience with cultural identity.

Working in acrylic, oil and mixed media, artist Kamrul Hasan Lipu moves between recognisable forms and abstraction. Layers of colour, free-flowing lines, marks and textures give different expressions to his subjects and feelings.

He completed an Advanced Diploma in Painting at the Toyo Institute of Art and Design in Tokyo in 2012. His art education and years in Japan have informed his continuing exploration of Bangladesh's people, nature and folk culture.

His previous group exhibitions include the 14th Yokohama Port Independent Exhibition in 2026 and the 29th Seya Art Exhibition that year, where he participated as an invited artist.

Alongside his painting practice, artist Kamrul Hasan Lipu is active in cultural work within the Bangladeshi community in Japan. He founded Kahal Art Group, a joint Bangladesh-Japan arts organisation.

Through Kahal Gallery, he has been involved in presenting artists from different countries, introducing Bangladeshi nakshi kantha and folk art, and organising cultural programmes marking Bangladesh's national days.

The exhibition catalogue includes messages from artists Rafiqun Nabi and Jamal Ahmed, Professor Shahjahan Ahmed Bikash, and Japanese graphic designer and art critic Ikufumi Fukuzawa. Their assessments address Lipu's sustained practice, use of colour and texture, cultural memory and experimentation.

The first solo exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to see several strands of artist Kamrul Hasan Lipu's practice together. Women's faces, water lilies, folk imagery and abstract arrangements of colour return to questions of memory, people and identity.

The exhibition at Gallery Shimizu is open daily from 11:00 am to 6:00 pm. On the final day, 25 October, Sunday, it closes at 4:00 pm.

item.title: Child abuse in madrasas: Will the ulema continue to remain silent?
item.description:
A teacher wearing a lungi and undershirt is mercilessly beating a child aged eight or nine with a thick stick held in both hands. When his arms grow tired, he kicks the child. Then, sitting in front of the child, he delivers repeated punches to the child’s face and stomach. Several children of the same age sit in a row, watching the scene in terror.

Countless people have seen this barbaric footage circulating on social media. I have seen it too.

Yet the scene is not new to me. I can still picture the second floor of the Gouranadi madrasa-mosque, where Mufti Huzur would beat us with all his might using a thick bamboo stick held in both hands. We little children watched our classmates writhe in pain and heard their piercing screams.

The students’ offence was that they had gone to watch a football match on television during the World Cup. And the stick in the teacher’s hands was actually a large ladle used to stir curry in an enormous cooking pot.

I remember the tip of a cane hurled by the teacher piercing Neyamat’s thigh, soaking the boy’s pyjama in blood. I remember a teacher kicking a child at one end of a huge hifz hall, a room for memorising the Quran, until the child rolled all the way to the other end. I remember heavy chunks of wood being chained to some children’s hands or feet to prevent them from escaping the madrasa.

The teachers were hardly remorseful. On the contrary, much like a teacher whose video has recently circulated on TikTok, showing him poking a child in the face with a cane and writing, “I really enjoy making children cry,” our teachers also made all sorts of callous jokes about the punishments they inflicted on students. Parents were even more extreme. When enrolling their children, they would tell the teachers, “Huzur, the flesh is yours, but the bones are mine,” implying they could punish them as long as they remained intact.

From physical abuse to sexual abuse

Physical punishment is not the only offence committed by madrasa teachers. Beyond fragmented discussions on social media, horrifying accounts of sexual abuse of children are now appearing in mainstream news media.

I suspect it would be difficult to find anyone who attended a madrasa in our time who had never heard of a teacher abusing a student. Today, cases of rape involving girls at female madrasas are also coming to light. There have even been allegations of killings following rape or of circumstances leading to suicide.

For example, on 19 May, the very day the Ramisa murder case was being discussed across the country, we saw reports of the body of Abdullah, a 10-year-old boy, hanging at a madrasa in Banasree. There were signs of sexual abuse around his anus. We also saw reports of a series of unnatural deaths at a female madrasa in Cumilla, with post-mortem examinations revealing signs of abuse. Teachers themselves have even been recording photographs or videos of children studying and posting them on social media with objectionable and suggestive comments.

It is therefore evident that child abuse in madrasas has evolved into a range of offences. These include: (1) physically punishing children; (2) raping boys; (3) raping girls; (4) killing children after abuse or creating circumstances that drive them to suicide; (5) recording acts of child abuse and posting them on social media; and (6) circulating children’s photographs or videos with objectionable comments. Each of these constitutes a serious offence under Bangladesh’s criminal law, with penalties ranging from a minimum of five years’ imprisonment to the death penalty.

Impunity and the evasion of institutional responsibility

Although laws exist, their enforcement in practice is quite the opposite—a case of rules existing on paper but not in reality.

An extreme example is the alleged sexual abuse of a nine-year-old student at a madrasa in Tangail Sadar.

According to the child’s parents, the madrasa’s headteacher would frighten children by invoking jinn and touch them on intimate parts of their bodies. He allegedly instructed them to record these acts on mobile phones. Although the accused teacher was arrested, he was released on bail just two months later and opened another madrasa under a new name—with the approval of the madrasa education board.

How was this possible?

When asked by Netra News about the matter, Maulana Nadvi, chief director of the Befaqul Madarisil Arabia, the leading board of Qawmi madrasas, said, “It may be that the new registration was obtained in a different name through someone else.”

Expressing his own helplessness, he added, “Legally, the board does not have the authority to do anything.” The question is: Does the board lack even the authority to hand an accused person over to the law enforcement authorities or take the initiative to file a case itself? Did it do either?

A few weeks later, he claimed on social media that, of 57 complaints concerning madrasas received over the previous three months, 52 were false and part of conspiracies. Yet he presented no evidence and did not consider it necessary to tell the media what kind of investigation had been conducted.

Why, after one case of child abuse, rape or murder after another, was the first priority of the institutions and boards to prove their own innocence rather than ensure accountability? Seeking an answer to this question reveals that the problem is not merely a matter of a few individuals with perverse tendencies; it reflects a deep structural failure.

Long-term data published by the Bangladesh Peace Observatory in The Daily Star indicate that most child abuse occurs within families or familiar environments. Hundreds of children are also being abused by teachers at schools, universities and private tutoring sessions, as well as at madrasas.

Therefore, the problem cannot simply be reduced to a “madrasa problem”. But that does not diminish the responsibility of madrasa authorities. The question is not about comparing rates of abuse. It is about the role institutions and boards play when crimes occur under their watch.

Criminological and psychological analysis

One established criminological theory is the “routine activity theory”. It holds that three elements must converge for a crime to occur: a person motivated to commit a crime, an accessible victim, and the absence of a capable guardian.

The existing structure of residential hifz institutions and madrasas makes all three conditions unusually easy to fulfil. Children are separated from their families; supervision is concentrated in the hands of one or two teachers; there is no independent third-party monitoring; and teachers’ absolute authority is treated as beyond question.

This is not an inherent defect of religious institutions. The risk increases in any closed institution with inadequate supervision and unchecked authority. Similar patterns have been observed worldwide in orphanages, boarding schools and sports academies. But failing to take measures to mitigate known structural risks creates serious institutional responsibility.

In psychology, this kind of tendency can be explained through the concept of “moral licensing”. Religious identity can create an aura around a person in the eyes of society, making it difficult for suspicion to take hold. A robe and cap, being a hafiz of the Quran, or being addressed as “Huzur” are all powerful symbols of trustworthiness in society. Offenders may consciously or unconsciously exploit this perception.

The madrasa in Tangail where a teacher allegedly touched children after frightening them with stories of jinn provides a classic example of this tactic. Fear and religious authority are combined to place a child in a psychological state in which resistance or disclosure may seem unimaginable.

When the truth finally comes out, the victim suffers a second injury if the institution refuses to believe the child and instead tries to cover up the incident.

Psychology calls this “institutional betrayal”, which can cause longer-lasting psychological harm than the original abuse itself.

Transparency versus the “burden of sacredness”

Against this backdrop, Befaqul Madarisil Arabia’s claim that the allegations amount to “propaganda” must be examined fairly.

The concern is not entirely unfounded: some allegations may be politically motivated or arise from misunderstandings, as in the case of Mozaffar, an innocent teacher from Netrokona who spent seven years in prison.

Likewise, the risk of sweeping allegations against religious institutions is real. But the solution is not to deny the truth; it is to ensure transparency. If claims of false allegations are genuine, the evidence should be presented through the findings of an independent investigation. Merely citing a number in a statement does not discharge one’s responsibility.

Another tension is at work here, which might be described in philosophical terms as the “burden of sacredness”. The more an institution becomes a symbol of religious sanctity, the more its criticism is liable to be misinterpreted as an “attack on religion”. This misunderstanding silences critics and gives offenders free rein. Islamic jurisprudence, however, offers an effective solution.

One recognised principle of fiqh, or Islamic jurisprudence, is ‘sadd al-dhara’i,’ meaning “blocking the means or pathways that may lead to harm”. This principle should have been applied in madrasas before anything else, yet it is absent in practice.

Has any madrasa authority set an example by handing over to the law the teacher seen brutally beating a child in the footage circulating on social media? Instead, the number of offences continues to rise amid the authorities’ indifference.

According to data from the human rights organisation Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), at least 52 children suffered sexual abuse in madrasas last year, three of whom died. Between 2020 and 2025, at least 211 incidents of rape and sexual abuse at madrasas across the country were reported in the media.

Human rights activists believe the actual number is higher because most incidents are suppressed through local informal arbitration.

International examples and the way forward

The problem of abuse in madrasas is not unique to Bangladesh. Similar patterns have emerged in other countries, but they have chosen the path of reform.

In Senegal, abuse had continued for years within daaras, residential Quranic education centres. Following a ruling by the international child rights body ACERWC in 2021, the state began a programme to bring daaras under the formal education system and develop what it called “modern daaras”.

In Pakistan, the leaking of a video in 2021 showing a senior teacher named Mufti Azizur Rahman raping someone triggered widespread outrage. Subsequently, madrasa boards introduced stricter codes of conduct, and the federal education ministry brought all madrasas under government registration.

In Indonesia, the ministries responsible for women and children’s affairs and religious affairs are working together to prevent abuse in Islamic boarding schools. Measures include establishing a child protection task force at every madrasa, installing confidential complaint boxes, setting up hotlines and making psychological screening mandatory for teacher recruitment.

Because Bangladesh’s Qawmi madrasas operate outside the government registration system, there are no background checks on teachers’ past records, no psychological screening and no independent mechanism to monitor compliance with the safeguards under the Children Act 2013.

To fill this gap, every madrasa must verify the backgrounds of teachers and staff, adopt policies restricting unsupervised one-to-one interactions, establish confidential complaint hotlines and set up independent child protection units recognised by the relevant boards. At the same time, non-residential alternatives to residential hifz programmes should be expanded for young children so that parents can remain regularly involved in their lives.

A similar instruction can be found in the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). When a group of adolescent boys and young men came to him to learn about religion, he permitted them to stay for no more than 20 days. Seeing how much they longed for their families, he affectionately told them: “Go back to your families, stay with them, teach them religious knowledge and enjoin good deeds. And pray as you have seen me pray” (Sahih Muslim, Hadith 631).

How, then, can it be justified to keep children aged six to 10 confined in enclosed rooms, separated from their families for years on end?

The safety of residential religious educational institutions cannot be left solely to the blind faith of parents. It is the responsibility of both the state and madrasa boards. If an institution, despite knowing the structural risks, focuses on protecting offenders rather than preventing or addressing abuse, its inaction amounts to nothing less than complicity in the crimes.

If the ulema do not clean up this rot within their own ranks, history will remember them not as guardians of religion but as silent accomplices to crime.

* Manzurul Haque is a senior sub-editor at Prothom Alo’s Religion Desk. Prothom Alo Bangla online published this article by Manzurul Haque on 29 July 2026. item.title: Police vehicle attacked, 3 officers assaulted during banned BCL-Jubo League Gopalganj march
item.description:
In Gopalganj Sadar Upazila, a police vehicle was attacked and vandalised from a rally organised by the banned Chhatra League and the Jubo League, whose activities are prohibited.

Chhatra League is the student wing and Jubo League the youth wing affiliated with Awami League whose activities are banned.

During this time, three police officers were assaulted.

This incident took place on Saturday afternoon in the Kheyaghat area of Raghunathpur union of Sadar Upazila.

Gopalganj's Superintendent of Police, Md Habibullah, confirmed this to Prothom Alo.

The injured individuals are Sub-Inspector (SI) Fulmia and Constables Shaukat and Jasim from the Sadar police station.

In a video spread on social media, a group of young individuals can be seen heading towards an intersection with a rally while chanting slogans like "Joy Bangla" and "Bangladesh will smile when Sheikh Hasina arrives. " They were seen carrying hockey sticks and split bamboo sticks.

A police vehicle was parked near the intersection, with the driver inside. Three police officers were standing nearby, one of whom was seen talking on a mobile phone and gesturing for the young men to move ahead with their rally. At one point, the youths in the rally began vandalising the police vehicle. The driver was inside during this time.

Amidst the vandalism, the driver started to drive the vehicle forward. At this time, the youths chased the vehicle and continued to vandalise it. A police officer was seen trying to restrain them. After the vehicle had moved a bit, the youths started attacking the police officers. Some of the youths were seen trying to stop the attackers. Despite this, some continued to beat the police officers. Eventually, the police officers ran to the vehicle and drove away.

Superintendent of Police Habibullah said that a team from Gopalganj Sadar police station was on regular patrol. In the afternoon, the police members were resting after stopping their vehicle in the Kheyaghat area of Raghunathpur Union.

At that time, leaders and activists of the Jubo League with prohibited activities and the banned Chhatra League came with a rally and attacked and vandalised the police vehicle. They had hockey sticks and indigenous weapons in their hands. At one point, they assaulted the police officers.

The Superintendent of Police further said that video footage from the scene showed that the police members were standing there and did not intervene with the rally participants. Despite this, the rally participants came and vandalised the police vehicle and attacked the police officers.

Additional Superintendent of Police of Gopalganj, Mohammad Kazi Humayun Rashid, stated that a process is underway to file a case regarding this incident. He mentioned that police operations to arrest the attackers are ongoing.

item.title: Lakshmi Puja on Sunday
item.description:
Lakshmi Puja, a major religious festival of the Hindu community, will be celebrated on Sunday with due religious fervour and enthusiasm.
The Puja takes place on the first full-moon night after the end of Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of Hindus.
This full-moon night is also called "Kujagori Purnima", and that is why this puja is also known as "Kujagori Lakshmi Puja".
Hindus believe that Goddess Lakshmi arrives to receive worship on the night of Purnima to give blessings of prosperity. In this belief, Bengali Hindus perform Lakshmi Puja in each of their houses.
In addition to the full moon in the month of Ashwin, some also perform special worship of Goddess Lakshmi every Thursday. In certain regions, there is a tradition of worshipping Lakshmi on the evening of "Dipanwita Amavasya" (the new moon night associated with Diwali). The worship is conducted using a ghat (a consecrated pot) or an idol, and it can be observed either individually or collectively.
According to the scriptures, Goddess Lakshmi is the embodiment of wealth and prosperity. She is revered as the deity of progress, light, knowledge, good fortune, fertility, generosity, courage and beauty truly the Goddess of Opulence.
The owl is the Bahan (divine vehicle) of Goddess Lakshmi. When Lord Vishnu incarnated as Rama and Krishna, Lakshmi accompanied him as Sita and Radha, respectively. On the night of Kojagari Purnima, it is believed that the Goddess Lakshmi visits the homes of her devotees to bless them with abundance and prosperity. Since ancient times, everyone from kings and monarchs to merchants and ordinary householders has worshipped Goddess Lakshmi.
According to the Vishuddha Siddhanta Panjika (the authoritative Hindu almanack), Kojagari Lakshmi Puja will be observed on Sunday. The Purnima Tithi (lunar day of the full moon) will begin at 11:55am on Monday and conclude at 9:41am on Tuesday.
In Bengali society, there are various popular tales centered on the Goddess Lakshmi. These stories, composed in the form of Panchali (narrative verses), are recited on the day of the Puja; this practice is known as "Lakshmi'r Panchali".
Essential items for Lakshmi Puja include vermilion (sindoor), a consecrated pot (ghat), unhusked rice (dhan), earth, mango leaves, flowers, durva grass, tulsi leaves, haritaki (myrobalan), sandalwood, incense, diya (lamps), naivedya (offerings of food), atap rice (sun-dried rice) and water.
During the Lakshmi Puja, the household courtyard is adorned with a mangalghat (a sacred pot) and sheaves of paddy, alongside alpona (traditional decorative patterns) made from rice flour, which often depict the footprints of Goddess Lakshmi. On this occasion, women observe a fast.
It is customary to stay awake throughout the night during Lakshmi Puja. The term "Kojagari" is derived from the question, "Who is awake?"
According to the scriptures, Goddess Lakshmi visits every home on this night. If the doors of a house are closed and the residents are asleep, she turns back. For this reason, the observance is known as "Kojagari" Lakshmi Puja, and there is a tradition of keeping an all-night vigil. Goddess Lakshmi is worshipped in the homes of Bengali Hindus; many families also perform a ritual worship of the Goddess every Thursday.
Many within the Hindu community observe a fast during Lakshmi Puja. In addition to the religious rituals, alpona patterns, specifically the footprints of Goddess Lakshmi are drawn in the courtyards of homes.

item.title: Thirteen arrested in anti-mugging drive in Mohammadpur
item.description:
Police have arrested 13 people, including a woman and three minors, in a special anti-mugging drive in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur, recovering locally made weapons and four stolen mobile phones.
The arrestees are Shanto Hossain Shahin, 21, Fahimul Hasan Alif, 22, Abir Bepari Shanto, 23, Rajib, 25, Md Arafat Rahman, 20, Md Hasnain Hasan, 26, Md Naim, 25, Naim Omar, 23, Md Swapan, 19, and Mosammat Khushi Akter, 19. The other three are minors.
According to Mohammadpur police, the arrests were made during special drives at different locations in the area on Friday.
Police recovered three switchblades, two sharp knives, 10 iron rods, a serrated knife and four stolen mobile phones.
Md Hasnain Hasan faces several mugging cases filed with Mohammadpur, Dhanmondi and Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police stations, police said.
According to preliminary findings, the group allegedly used weapons to intimidate pedestrians, bus and rickshaw passengers, and relatives of patients visiting hospitals before snatching their mobile phones, cash and other valuables.
The group also allegedly targeted female pedestrians, stealing mobile phones and other belongings from their bags when they were distracted.
Two separate cases have been filed against the arrestees with Mohammadpur Police Station. The process of producing them before a court is underway, police said.

item.title: Bangladesh seeks grant-based climate finance ahead of COP31
item.description:
Bangladesh’s position at the upcoming United Nations climate conference will depend on coordinated efforts across government, the private sector and civil society, alongside demands for developed countries to provide climate finance through grants rather than loans.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam stressed the need for collective action to strengthen the country’s negotiating position and urged developed nations to fulfil their climate finance commitments without adding to the debt burden of vulnerable countries.
She made the remarks as the chief guest at a national dialogue titled “People-Led Policy: Bangladesh Position at COP31” at the CIRDAP auditorium in Dhaka on Saturday.
Organized jointly by 33 national and international organizations working on climate change in Bangladesh, the dialogue presented key demands and recommendations from a civil society position paper ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).
Shama Obaed said Bangladesh needed to assess progress in implementing climate commitments a decade after the Paris Agreement, stressing that climate-vulnerable countries required adequate financial support to address the impacts of global warming.
She called for equal attention to adaptation and mitigation, greater transparency in international climate negotiations and stronger coordination among stakeholders to bridge the gap between Bangladesh’s expectations and negotiating outcomes.
The state minister said initiatives were underway to strengthen coordination between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change. She also expressed interest in involving young climate advocates in the process.
Highlighting opportunities to promote sustainable products, she said Bangladesh planned to showcase environmentally friendly jute products at COP31 through a dedicated Jute Pavilion. The initiative could help expand international markets and improve the livelihoods of rural farmers.
Mirza Shawkat Ali, director of Climate Change and International Convention at the Department of Environment, attended the dialogue as a special guest.
He said initiatives were being taken to reduce industrial emissions, adding that credible evidence and specific action plans were essential to presenting Bangladesh’s demands effectively in international negotiations.
In his welcome address, Dr S M Munjurul Hannan Khan, executive director of Nature Conservation Management (NACOM), stressed the need for coordinated planning on climate finance, the blue economy, waste management and urban heat stress.
Farah Kabir, country director of ActionAid Bangladesh and moderator of the dialogue, called for collective efforts to secure grant-based climate finance.
She said Bangladesh was among the countries disproportionately affected by climate change and that international support should not deepen the debt burden of vulnerable countries and communities.
Presentations at the dialogue outlined Bangladesh’s climate financing requirements and the challenges of implementing its climate commitments.
According to figures presented at the event, Bangladesh’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) targets a 20.31% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, equivalent to 84.97 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent.
Implementation of the plan for 2026-2035 is estimated to require $116.18 billion, including $90.23 billion in international support.
Meanwhile, the National Adaptation Plan for 2023-2050 identifies 113 initiatives requiring approximately $230 billion.
Roufa Khanum of the Centre for Climate Change and Environmental Research (C3ER) presented figures on global emissions and Bangladesh’s climate risks.
Professor Dr Ahmad Kamruzzaman Majumder, chairman of the Centre for Atmospheric Pollution Studies (CAPS), highlighted the need for improved waste management and measures to curb air pollution and industrial emissions.
Mahzabeen Mahfuz of ActionAid Bangladesh discussed a just energy transition, while Chowdhury Abrar Zahin and Helena Khatun addressed marine resources and international finance.
Youth representatives presented 6 demands covering climate finance, education, employment, gender justice and meaningful participation in decision-making.
The discussion emphasized that climate finance must reach affected communities and that people displaced by climate change should receive adequate resettlement support.
Participants also called for the meaningful involvement of women, persons with disabilities, young people and other marginalized groups in climate policymaking and national delegations.
The civil society position paper outlined several priorities for Bangladesh at COP31, including securing debt-free, grant-based international climate finance to implement NDC 3.0 and strengthening coordination among the government, civil society, young people and the private sector.
It also called for promoting green innovation and environmentally friendly domestic products, reducing industrial emissions and ensuring a just energy transition that protects workers.
Other priorities include securing financing for safe housing for climate migrants, improving urban waste management and addressing extreme heat in cities.
The recommendations underscore the need for Bangladesh to pursue a unified negotiating position combining climate finance demands with stronger adaptation measures, environmental protection and the rights of communities most affected by climate change.

item.title: Biman doubles Dhaka-Narita flights ahead of PM's Japan visit
item.description:
Biman Bangladesh Airlines has decided to double its weekly flights between Dhaka and Japan's Narita from Thursday, coinciding with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's official visit to Japan, a senior airline official said on Saturday.
"We are increasing the frequency on the Dhaka-Narita-Dhaka route from one to two flights a week, with the additional service beginning on October 29," Biman's Director (Marketing and Sales) Md Ashraful Alam told BSS.
He said the national flag carrier would operate flights on the route every Monday and Thursday, strengthening direct air connectivity between Bangladesh and Japan.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would travel to Japan on Biman's regular commercial flight for his four-day official visit beginning Monday.
"The prime minister will also return home on Thursday aboard Biman's newly introduced Thursday flight from Narita," Alam said.
The decision to increase flight frequency comes nearly three months after Biman resumed its direct Dhaka-Narita-Dhaka service on July 27 this year, restoring Bangladesh's only nonstop air connection with Japan following a suspension of more than a year.
The airline initially relaunched the route with one weekly flight using a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner, with plans to increase frequencies depending on passenger demand, commercial performance and aircraft availability.
Earlier, Biman officials said the resumption of direct flights had received an encouraging response from passengers, particularly Bangladeshis living in Japan.
More than 40,000 Bangladeshi students and workers are estimated to be living in Japan, creating growing demand for direct air travel between the two countries.
The route is also considered important for expanding bilateral trade, investment, tourism and people-to-people exchanges.
Biman is exploring potential codeshare arrangements with Japan Airlines (JAL) and Air Canada to establish Narita as a transit gateway for Bangladeshi passengers travelling to North America and other destinations in the Asia-Pacific region.
If finalized, the proposed partnerships could enable passengers to travel beyond Narita to destinations such as Vancouver, Los Angeles and Seoul through connecting services under coordinated ticketing and baggage arrangements.
The Dhaka-Narita route was originally relaunched in September 2023 after a 17-year suspension but was discontinued on July 1, 2025, amid aircraft shortages, operational costs and commercial considerations.
Following the formation of the current BNP government, Biman moved to restore the service as part of broader efforts to strengthen Bangladesh-Japan economic and aviation cooperation.
The latest decision to introduce a second weekly flight is expected to provide greater travel flexibility for passengers while supporting the national carrier's efforts to strengthen the route's commercial sustainability.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to pay an official visit to Japan from Monday to Thursday at the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
During the visit, the two countries are expected to hold high-level bilateral talks and explore opportunities to expand cooperation in trade, investment, infrastructure, aviation and human resource development.

item.title: Tongi child abuse case: Father vows to fight charges
item.description:
The father of a six-year-old girl allegedly sexually abused at a residential madrasa in Tongi’s Auchpara has vowed to fight the case filed against him while respecting the law, and demanded a fair investigation into the alleged abuse of his daughter.
Shahjalal Rumi made the remarks at a press conference around 3:00am on Saturday amid growing controversy over the incident. His friend and content creator Taj was also present.
Rumi said he went to the madrasa to seek justice for his daughter, not to create a mob.
“I went to the madrasa to seek justice for my child, not to create a mob. The authorities are claiming that I created a mob and went there to occupy a flat. Why would I do that?” he said.
“If I had created a mob, there were more than 50 people there. Why didn’t they all attack me? I went there as a father seeking justice for my child,” he added.
Rumi said he was not against the madrasa or its teachers, noting that he had sent his daughter there to receive religious education.
“I am not against Islam or genuine religious scholars. I am speaking against those who use religious identity to commit crimes and try to hide the truth,” he said.
Rumi said he had been unable to sleep properly since learning about the alleged abuse.
He claimed that he had informed the madrasa principal about the incident three days earlier but received no response.
“I waited outside his room for a long time. When I finally spoke to him, he behaved as if he did not want to meet me,” Rumi said.
He also alleged that the accused teacher had threatened the child, warning her that she would be killed if she told anyone at home. Frightened, the girl remained silent for three days before eventually telling her mother, he said.
Rumi said the madrasa authorities had previously assured him that CCTV cameras would be installed in the rooms to ensure the safety of female students. Based on that assurance, he had sent his daughter back to the madrasa.
He further claimed that the accused had later messaged the child’s maternal grandfather, saying he would not commit such an offence again.
Regarding the case filed against him, Rumi said, “I learned in the afternoon that a case had been filed against me. If the law considers me guilty, I will accept whatever punishment is prescribed. I respect the law and will fight the case. But I also want justice for what happened to my child.”
Rejecting allegations that he had taken Tk17 lakh from the madrasa, Rumi called for the institution’s CCTV footage to be examined.
“The madrasa has CCTV cameras. Let the footage be checked to see where I allegedly took Tk17 lakh from. It should also be clarified how such a large amount of money was kept at the madrasa,” he said.
He urged the authorities to investigate all allegations against him fairly.
Addressing the public, Rumi said: “If what allegedly happened to my daughter had happened to your own child, would you have accepted it?”
He appealed for public support to ensure his daughter’s safety and justice, urging people not to blindly trust individuals or institutions based on their identity, but to verify allegations through an impartial investigation.

item.title: Health minister orders nurse transfer, salary cuts for four doctors
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Saturday paid a surprise visit to Phulpur Upazila Health Complex in the district and ordered transfer of a nurse for negligence of duty.
He also directed deduction of one day’s salary of four doctors for remaining absent from their workplace without prior permission, said a press release.
After the inspection, the health minister told journalists that the government is working to bring the country’s health sector to a level that meets public expectations and ensures people’s satisfaction, in line with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directives.
Noting that the government has taken various initiatives to resolve long-standing problems in the health sector, he said, “Cleanliness activities at hospitals are being strengthened, medicine supplies are being increased and adequate stocks of saline have been ensured.”
Sakhawat expressed the hope that significant progress in the health sector would become visible within the next few months.
He also said the government plans to invite tenders worth several thousand crore taka within the next 15 days as part of its efforts to develop and restructure the health sector.
This tender is aimed at improving various healthcare institutions across the country, including upazila health complexes, the minister said.
Besides, he said, initiatives are being taken to establish modern pathological laboratories at upazila-level hospitals so that diagnostic facilities can be expanded at the grassroots level.
Later, the minister made another surprise visit to the nearby Tarakanda Upazila Health Complex in Mymensingh.

item.title: Two killed, 15 injured in bus-truck collision in Brahmanbaria
item.description:
Two passengers were killed and 15 others injured in a head-on collision between a passenger bus and a truck in the Bertala area of Sarail upazila in Brahmanbaria on Saturday morning.
The accident occurred at around 8:30am on the Dhaka-Sylhet Highway. The deceased were identified as Sourav and Asif, both from Parbatipur in Dinajpur. However, Asif’s full identity could not be confirmed. Of the injured, 3 were sent to Dhaka in critical condition.
Police and local residents said a passenger bus operated by Diganta Paribahan, traveling from Rangpur to Sylhet, collided head-on with a truck coming from the opposite direction in the Berotola area of Sarail upazila.
Several passengers sustained serious injuries in the collision. They were rescued and taken to hospital, while 3 critically injured passengers were sent to Dhaka for advanced treatment.
Abdul Halim, officer-in-charge of Khatihata Highway Police Station, said police were sent to the scene immediately after the accident. The vehicles, which were severely damaged in the collision, were taken into police custody.

item.title: Traditional Bou Mela brings communities together to find life partners in Dinajpur
item.description:
The centuries-old Adivasi Bou Mela, popularly known as the 'Bride Fair', brought hundreds of young men and women from indigenous communities together at Golapganj High School ground in Birganj upazila of Dinajpur district on Friday, blending traditional matchmaking with cultural festivities.
The annual fair, held a day or two after Durga Puja, featured traditional dances, folk music, colourful attire and temporary stalls selling daily necessities, cosmetics and other items. People from different religious and social backgrounds, including Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist and Christian communities, also attended the event, which continued until 11pm.
At the heart of the fair is an opportunity for eligible young men and women to meet prospective life partners in a familiar cultural setting. According to the organisers, more than 400 eligible youths from indigenous communities were identified as prospective matches this year.
The participants interacted and exchanged views, while any subsequent marriage arrangements would be pursued through discussions between the respective families. Organisers expressed hope that some of the prospective matches would lead to marriages within the next one or two months.
The fair also provided a platform for indigenous communities to showcase their cultural heritage and maintain social ties. Young women in colourful saris performed traditional dances, while visitors enjoyed music and other cultural activities.
Indigenous community leader Joks Tudu said that the participating communities included Santals, Paharis, Oraons, Malos and other indigenous groups.
He said growing access to education and increased social awareness had brought significant changes to indigenous communities, with many young people pursuing higher education and adapting to modern social and professional life while retaining their cultural traditions.
However, the longstanding matchmaking custom has also prompted debate among some younger members of the communities.
Indigenous leader and schoolteacher Habib Lakra said that a small number of young people had recently expressed interest in changing aspects of the tradition.
He referred to discussions on social media, including Facebook, where individuals such as Rita Hemrom and Albericuz Hazda had shared their views on the practice.
The debate reflects differing views on how the tradition can be preserved while accommodating changing social values and individual choices in matters of marriage.
The fair was formally inaugurated on Friday afternoon by Birganj Upazila Nirbahi Officer Suma Khatun at a ceremony presided over by Joseph Hembram, convener of the Adivasi Samaj Unnayan Samiti.
Rejwanul Islam Rizu, an adviser to the Dinajpur district unit of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, a director of the Dinajpur Chamber of Commerce and president of the upazila brick kiln owners' association, attended as a special guest.
A preparatory meeting was held ahead of the event, with local lawmaker Md Manjurul Islam providing guidance on its organisation.
Dinajpur Superintendent of Police Md Zedan Al Musa said that the fair concluded peacefully and in an orderly manner despite the large turnout of indigenous people from across the northern region.
Beyond matchmaking, the Adivasi Bou Mela continues to serve as a meeting place for communities to celebrate their heritage, strengthen social ties and engage with changing social realities while preserving a longstanding cultural tradition.

item.title: Madhumati embankment breach sparks erosion fears
item.description:
A 52-metre section of a protective embankment along the Madhumati River has developed a breach near Fukra Launch Ghat in Gopalganj’s Kashiani upazila, raising fears of further erosion and threatening nearby homes, farmland, roads and institutions.
Built about 10 years ago, the 2.5km embankment had helped bring river erosion under control. However, a breach that appeared on September 23 has renewed concerns among residents, who are demanding permanent protection.
Several other sections of the embankment are also at risk, as the soil beneath the structure is suspected to have been washed away.
The Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) began placing sandbags at the site on October 10. Around 5,000 sandbags have been placed to contain the erosion, said Md Koushik Gazi, a work assistant at the BWDB’s Bhatia Para sub-divisional engineer’s office in Kashiani.
He said the river’s narrow, deep channel and a bend near Fukra Launch Ghat had contributed to the problem. As water levels began to recede about a month ago, the current intensified, triggering the breach.
The full extent of the damage would become clear once water levels fell further, allowing officials to assess the condition of the embankment, Gazi added.
BWDB Gopalganj Executive Engineer Md Shawkat Osman said temporary measures were underway to prevent further erosion, while a feasibility study for permanent protection was in progress.
“Once the study is completed, we plan to construct a permanent protective embankment near Fukra Launch Ghat under a project,” he said.
Local residents Md Mintu Munshi and Alamgir Hossain Zakir said erosion had already destroyed homes, farmland and trees in the area. They said nearly two kilometres of land on the Gopalganj side had been eroded, while chars had emerged across the river in Lohagara upazila of Narail.
The renewed erosion has put remaining homes, cropland, roads and educational and religious institutions at risk, they said, urging the authorities to build a permanent embankment.
Abir Alamgir Piyas, a first-year honours student at Ramdia SK Government College, said generations of local residents had lost their ancestral land to river erosion.
“The erosion has started again, putting whatever property we have left at risk. My family and many others are living in fear,” he said, calling for permanent protection.

item.title: Banned Chhatra League, Jubo League activists attack police in Gopalganj, injure 2
item.description:
Leaders and activists of the banned Chhatra League and Jubo League attacked police in Gopalganj on Saturday afternoon, vandalizing a police vehicle and beating 2 police personnel, according to police.
The incident took place around noon in the Raghunathpur ferry terminal area of Gopalganj Sadar upazila. Activists of the 2 organizations were seen taking part in the attack with sticks.
A video of the incident has circulated on social media, with several Chhatra League activists who took part in the procession sharing it on their Facebook accounts.
The video shows processionists carrying sticks from Charpara road in Raghunathpur and arriving at the ferry terminal area. They chanted “Joy Bangla” before attacking and vandalizing a police vehicle on patrol. Police personnel left the scene in the vehicle immediately after the vandalism.
Gopalganj Sadar police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Aminul Islam said: “Police were conducting routine patrols in the Bedgram ferry terminal area under Sadar police station. At that time, several people were marching in support of Sheikh Hasina, led by banned Jubo League leader Milan and Chhatra League leader Mursalin. When police tried to stop them, the processionists attacked the police with sticks. 2 police personnel, including Sadar police station Sub-Inspector Phul Mia, were injured. The police vehicle was also vandalized. The officers then left the scene in the vehicle.”
The OC further said: “The 2 injured police personnel received primary treatment at Gopalganj 250-bed General Hospital. An operation is underway to arrest members of the banned Jubo League and Chhatra League involved in the attack and vehicle vandalism. Additional police have been deployed in the area.”
Senior police officials visited the scene after receiving news of the attack. The area remained tense following the incident.
Police and other law enforcement personnel have strengthened security measures and set up checkpoints at key locations across the district to maintain normalcy following the attack and vandalism.

item.title: Iran says US military not allowed to enter Gulf ‘under any circumstances’
item.description:
Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf “under any circumstances” and President Donald Trump will “take that dream to his grave.”
The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkiye Tom Barrack warned that Washington could “absolutely” strike Iran as soon as this weakened.
“We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time,” said Iran’s armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
“The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave.”
Iranian forces have restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit and gateway to the Gulf, since the war with the United States broke out on February 28.
In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships.
Tehran has required vessels to seek permission to transit, and repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern route close to the Omani coast.
According to the Guards, several tankers attempting to transit Hormuz through the route Tehran considers “illegal” were hit by mines in recent days.
On Friday, the Guards said two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil have been abandoned at sea after hitting mines in the strategic waterway.
“Their engine rooms were disabled by an explosion and a fierce fire,” the Guards said in a statement carried by their Sepah News website.
In peacetime, around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas passed through Hormuz.

item.title: Saudi forces launch deadly strikes on Yemen
item.description:
Saudi forces launched deadly airstrikes on Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa city and its surrounding governorate on Saturday, media associated with the Iran-backed group said, while also reporting around 20 strikes on Mocha.
The Houthis’ Al-Masirah reported a series of “Saudi enemy airstrikes” targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that killed at least three people and wounded several others.
A separate strike at a cement factory in the Sanaa governorate resulted in “a number of martyrs and wounded”, the broadcaster said.
The reports came after the Saudi coalition fighting in Yemen announced it had intercepted two missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif and Yanbu, in the kingdom’s west.
Earlier, Riyadh’s civil defense agency broadcast warnings of “potential danger” for four western Saudi regions, including Taif and Yanbu as well as Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest city, and Jeddah.
Riyadh leads a military coalition that first intervened in the conflict, which has devastated Yemen and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, in 2015.
The war had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war roiled the region.

item.title: Elon Musk has a lot to lose at US midterms as pollsters tip blue wave
item.description:
Last November, Elon Musk was looking to step away from the halls of power.
“You know, I’ve generally found that when I get involved in politics, it ends up badly,” he told investor and YouTuber Nikhil Kamath.
“Best to avoid where possible.”
The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive’s stint as a special government employee leading the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) had ended months earlier after a string of controversies.
Mr Musk also quietly shelved plans to launch a political party, which had been announced during a short-lived feud with US President Donald Trump.
But as the country’s midterm elections approach, Mr Musk is making another foray into politicking.
And as control of Congress is now within reach for Democrats, the stakes for the trillionaire are higher than ever.
With Mr Trump’s approval rating at record lows, Democrats are banking on breakthrough performances at the November 3 elections.
Forecasters say the House of Representatives is all but guaranteed to flip blue, while the Senate result is, at the least, a toss-up.
Despite arguing that “they never poll us right,” the president has embarked on a campaign blitz across the country.
He has also promised to pay every American adult $US5,000 if Republicans retain control of Congress, reminiscent of the $US5,000 cheques cut from DOGE savings once floated in early 2025.
Mr Musk may be staying off the campaign trail, but behind the scenes, he has become the biggest known midterm donor, sinking about $US442 million into Republican groups in this election cycle.
At least $US158 million of that has gone toward a race in his home state of Texas, in which Republicans are at risk of losing a once-safe US Senate seat to Democratic candidate James Talarico.
Mr Talarico’s campaign has released ads claiming Mr Musk wants to “buy his own US senator” by bankrolling Republican candidate Ken Paxton.
“So let’s remind Elon: Texas is not for sale,” the ads say.
Separately, Mr Musk earlier this month said he would give a SpaceX share to “every child in America” in 2027. While he did not provide details of the giveaway, Mr Trump claimed it as a victory for his Trump accounts program, through which he said the stock would be distributed.
There is a lot at stake for Mr Musk if control of the House changes over.
Democrats have been calling for investigations into several areas of his dealings, and if they win back gavels in several congressional committees, they will have the power to follow through.
Mr Musk recently landed himself in Democrats’ sights after Ukraine reported its access to the SpaceX owned Starlink and Starshield services had been restricted, affecting the country’s ability to defend against Russian drone attacks.
In response to the matter, Mr Musk said Starshield’s systems were controlled by the US government.
Mr Trump and the SpaceX owner have denied responsibility, but a Wall Street Journal report cited officials and people familiar with the matter as saying Mr Musk ordered the throttled speeds.
Days prior, Mr Musk commented that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had “gone too far” by striking Russian oil refineries.
US Representative Pramila Jayapal, a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, told Politico the incident raised questions about Mr Musk’s power.
“What happens when one guy gets a giant contract from the government and then uses it to do something that shuts down communication in a war that has been extremely important to the United States to support Ukraine?” she said.
“There’s a lot of different parts of the corruption around Musk.”
Democrats on several committees have also earmarked DOGE for congressional scrutiny.
Through its 10-month lifespan, the department cut an estimated 250,000 federal jobs, allegedly accessed sensitive data, and withheld congressionally appropriated funds.
Democrats have also alleged conflicts of interest between Mr Musk and the federal government.
Republicans blocked previous attempts by Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform to subpoena Mr Musk.
“There’s any number of House committees that would have jurisdiction in some respect over him,” said Harry Melkonian, an honorary associate at the United States Studies Centre.
“He’s a major defense contractor and Nasa contractor, so his companies receive staggering amounts of federal money each year.”
In June 2025, representative Jasmine Crockett, who sits on the oversight committee, vowed to “bring Elon Musk in” once Democrats regained the majority.
“And we can have him under oath, and we can have him tell us about everything that he did,” she said in an appearance on MSNBC.
In response to the Politico report that Democrats were discussing possible investigations into Mr Musk, the trillionaire threatened to retaliate against congressional investigations.
“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” he wrote on X.
“Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.”
Mr Musk could be called to testify at committee hearings and required to produce documents under a congressional investigation.
“For somebody like Musk, it would be truly awful to be sitting for eight hours a day, having a panel of people just questioning everything you do,” Dr Melkonian said.
“It becomes television news … and he is a businessman selling consumer products.”
But refusing to cooperate would present its own problems.
“On the political side, as a major contractor, he would be reluctant to antagonize a congressional majority because his companies depend on money voted by Congress,” Dr Melkonian said.
“Legally, he could be held in contempt of Congress.”
The federal misdemeanor is punishable by imprisonment of up to 12 months.
If an investigation uncovers any wrongdoing, the findings can be referred to the Department of Justice for prosecution.
The US attorney would be bound to take the matter to a grand jury in Washington, DC.
Dr Melkonian said the findings could lead Congress to determine Mr Musk as unfit for further dealings with the government.
“They could say, ‘We’re not going to authorize any more spending [on government contracts with Musk]’. That’s their ultimate power. Congress controls the dollars,” he said.
“Whether or not it ever goes to a federal judge, I don’t think he likes that.”

item.title: Ahead of APEC summit, Trump comes knocking on Kim’s door
item.description:
As world leaders prepare to gather in Shenzhen for November’s APEC summit, speculation is mounting over a possible meeting between Donald Trump and Kim Jong Un -- a prospect experts say remains remote.
In 2019, North Korea’s Kim made the 60-hour train journey home from Hanoi empty-handed after his summit with the US president collapsed.
Now, the dynamic has reversed: Trump is making repeated overtures, only to be met with silence from Pyongyang.
Trump said again last week that he “may” meet with Kim during his Asian tour next month and that it “would be exciting.”
But on Monday, he said: “I don’t know... I’m not sure that anybody’s asking for a meeting,” adding that his “relationship with Kim Jong Un is very good.”
Any meeting between the leaders would trigger a media frenzy, but Pyongyang’s deepening ties with Russia and China could complicate Trump’s bid for a potential announcement of talks ahead of the midterms.
Analysts say the mercurial US leader is seeking a foreign policy win as the Iran war drags on. Kim, by contrast, may have less to gain from another high-profile encounter with Trump, they say.
Kim’s decision to send troops and weapons to aid Moscow’s war in Ukraine has won critical backing from Russian President Vladimir Putin, helping North Korea blunt UN sanctions over its nuclear program.
North Korea’s economy, in fact, grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, South Korea’s central bank estimated in July, citing Pyongyang’s “expansion of economic cooperation with Russia” as its major driver.
China, Washington’s archrival, remains North Korea’s key ally -- a major source of diplomatic and economic support for the country.
“I see almost no possibility of a meeting,” Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
“For Kim Jong Un, maintaining the status quo is the best option right now.”
And last week, Seoul’s ambassador to Washington, Kang Kyung-wha, said no concrete progress had been made toward a meeting between Kim and Trump.
Trump met Kim three times during his first term -- once declaring they were “in love” -- in high-profile summits aimed at securing a denuclearization deal, but no tangible progress was made.
Since then, North Korea has continued to expand and develop its arsenal.
South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung -- who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions -- suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief.
Critics say such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.
Analysts say China has also appeared to move towards implicit acceptance.
Kim hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Pyongyang in June, soon after Xi held back-to-back summits in Beijing with Trump and Putin.
Neither Pyongyang nor Beijing mentioned North Korean denuclearisation in their official statements -- an omission experts saw as a sign of China’s tacit consent.
The dividing of the “United States and Japan on one side and North Korea, China and Russia on the other ... into blocs, is creating significant opportunities for North Korea,” Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, told AFP.
Pyongyang has repeatedly made clear it is no longer prepared to discuss denuclearisation.
Kim’s powerful sister Kim Yo Jong said in September the country’s nuclear-armed status was “absolute” and called those hoping for its denuclearisation “idiots.”
The more consequential question is “whether Washington would begin negotiating on the operational assumption that North Korea’s arsenal is not going to disappear,” Vladimir Tikhonov, Korean Studies professor at the University of Oslo, told AFP.
“I see that a possibility of such a policy shift is substantial.”
Meanwhile, China’s influence rests partly on its role as an intermediary between Pyongyang and Washington, analysts say, and a direct Trump-Kim deal that sidelines Beijing in Shenzhen could therefore erode its leverage over both sides.
“A dialogue may be pursued with the understanding of Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping,” said Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies.
But with Russia delivering immediate benefits, analysts said that time and strategic momentum are on Kim’s side.
“Giving up all these benefits, withdrawing from the Russia-Ukraine war, and entering uncertain dialogue with the United States is difficult to imagine right now,” Yang said.

item.title: Police fire tear gas as new French protests kick off
item.description:
French police started firing tear gas at protesters Saturday as they stepped up security in major cities aiming to prevent a repeat of rioting a week ago, on a day of fresh nationwide demonstrations over the high cost of living.
Police in the southeast city of Lyon fired tear gas to disperse some 150 protesters near the city center -- where demonstrations had been banned -- when they briefly tried to block a road, an AFP journalist saw.
“The police are really mobile... They come and disperse marches before they even form,” said a 21-year-old student who had turned up to protest, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Elsewhere, authorities and rattled shopkeepers geared up for potential new street violence.
Near Paris’s Bastille neighborhood, a clothing store had removed all its merchandise from shelves ahead of the demonstrations, while a nearby restaurant was boarded up with signs insisting it was “still open.” Many other retailers in the capital also had wooden boards covering their windows.
The Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay museums were closed.
The capital’s police said at midday officers had confiscated “various forbidden items” but described the situation as “calm.”
In Marseille, riot squad vehicles, armored trucks and a water cannon were parked in the city center, while police elsewhere prepared for potential clashes.
They were among 70,000 security personnel the interior ministry said were mobilized to counter the “high” threat of violence.
Adding to tensions, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party held a congress in Orleans to launch her campaign for elections in six months to choose President Emmanuel Macron’s successor.
Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched on Saturday against Le Pen, and also against Macron, a pro-business centrist leader. “Macron resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd yelled. Police put their numbers at 11,000 while organizers said 26,000 took part.
The unrest highlighted tensions in France ahead of the vote, which Le Pen is best-placed, according to surveys, to win.
Last weekend saw rioters on the margins of the nationwide demonstrations clash with police, vandalize public buildings and loot hundreds of stores. Some 2,700 people were arrested and the retail sector said shopowners were left with damage and stolen stock totaling hundreds of millions of euros.
Macron attributed the worst of the violence to “ultra-left” groups that he said “want to bring down the republic.”
Groups organizing Saturday’s renewed demonstrations have accused Macron and his government of ignoring widespread public anger over rising costs, and over classroom conditions for students.
Inflation in France, as elsewhere, has been sent surging by the Middle East war, started in February against Iran by US President Donald Trump and Israel.
Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has mobilized 500 troops to Milan after street violence there.
In Paris, streets on Saturday were unusually quiet, with many shop windows boarded up, and some of the bigger retailers sent messages to customers warning that they were closed for the day.
The capital’s police at the last minute ordered a union-organized march in the city be moved from Bastille, in the center-east, to the more remote eastern Porte d’Italie on the southern rim of the capital.
Unions said they reluctantly would go along with that.
But the Yellow Vests, who staged disruptive protests against Macron eight years ago, denounced an “authoritarian drift” and called for yet more demonstrations on October 31 for “the freedom to protest.”
A shopworker in the city of Rennes told AFP: “Bans are sometimes worse. Protesting is a right, and when you ban it you make it even more tempting.”
Macron and his government have sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday.
Courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, officials said.
Macron has said authorities would accept only union-led demonstrations and would counter any others they deemed “illegitimate.”
The restrictions, including outright bans on protests in some cities, have drawn criticism.
Amnesty International denounced what it called “a slide toward authoritarian practice,” saying the measures were “jeopardizing the right to demonstrate peacefully.”
“Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch.

item.title: Bothered by tiny “Chinese Cockroaches”?
item.description:
This is a very common problem in every household. Suddenly, tiny cockroaches are showing up around the kitchen sink, behind the fridge, in the corners of the wardrobe, or on the dining table! Though small, they breed quickly and can spread throughout the entire house. They are commonly called “Chinese cockroaches,” but to be sure which species they actually are, you need a photo or an expert’s identification.
Cockroaches can enter your home through grocery bags brought from outside, cartons, old furniture, used electronics, or even from a neighbor’s apartment. They can also travel around pipes in an apartment building, through gaps in the walls, and across various joints and connection points. The warmth of the kitchen, along with humidity and easy access to food, creates an ideal place for them to survive.
Cockroaches can survive on the tiniest food crumbs, oil and grease stains, dirt, and water. If their egg cases stay hidden in a safe spot, new cockroaches can hatch. Some species multiply significantly within just a few months. So it is not wise to ignore the problem after seeing only one or two cockroaches.
When people in the house fall asleep at night, cockroaches come out in search of food. Food left out overnight, dirty dishes, water droplets collecting in the sink, and leftovers in the trash bin all become easy food sources for them.
Remember, sweeping the house alone won’t be enough. If you can cut off the cockroaches’ sources of food and water, you can greatly reduce their chances of multiplying.
