item.title: Bangladesh Bank website restored after 3-day shutdown over cyberattack fears
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank’s official website was taken offline last Thursday amid fears of a cyberattack. It was restored at 8:00 am today, Sunday, after three days.

However, internet banking and mobile banking transactions continued as normal over the past three days, so customers faced no disruption to their transactions.

Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Arif Hossain Khan told Prothom Alo Sunday that the website had been checked for possible vulnerabilities. The decision to take it offline was made amid fears of attacks worldwide. As the risk has subsided, the website has been restored, he said.

Bangladesh Bank website shut down to prevent cyberattacks

The internet and software are now essential for operating government services, banking, e-commerce, news outlets and various online platforms. A large proportion of these websites rely on the PHP programming language.

The recent discovery of two serious security vulnerabilities in PHP has raised global concerns about cybersecurity.

According to reports by the BBC and Reuters, governments in various countries have taken emergency measures after two serious security vulnerabilities were identified in PHP, a widely used programming language for building and operating websites.

After news of the vulnerabilities emerged, governments and commercial organisations around the world began shutting down their websites from Wednesday night. Despite these measures, reports in various media outlets indicate that millions of hacking attempts have been made.

PHP flaws: Bangladesh Bank, land services, six banks’ websites remain offline

item.title: Thousands rally in Israel capital against Netanyahu ahead of vote
item.description:
ISRAEL-ELECTION/RALLY

Thousands gathered in Tel Aviv on Saturday for a large anti-government demonstration, three days ahead of a general election widely viewed as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by Palestinian militants on 7 October, 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas attack that sparked the Gaza war.

According to Israeli media, the gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu and who received a warm reception from the crowd.

"Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry," the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.

The latest polls published before a gag period entered into force on Friday night showed that neither bloc would obtain a majority of seats in Israel's parliament. A poll published by public broadcaster KAN found that out of 120 seats in the Israeli parliament, 52 would go to Eisenkot's bloc and 50 to Netanyahu's, with the rest going to non-aligned parties, including Arab ones.

An AFP reporter said thousands were marching from the central Rabin Square towards Hostages Square, a focal point for past anti-government protests to demand the release of those held captive in Gaza.

Israel's Netanyahu denounces enemies, allies in fiery UN speech

"Whoever has been leading us for the past four years (since Netanyahu's government took office in late 2022) has done such a terrible job," Hadas Feuershtein, 68, told AFP shortly before the start of the rally.

"Israel has never been in a situation as it is now," she added.

Ahead of the rally, the October Council had alerted law enforcement of possible "provocations" from pro-government agitators.

The Israeli police said on Saturday evening that it "arrested a suspect for assaulting the security team of a public figure" in Tel Aviv, with the Israeli press identifying the target as former Prime Minister and opposition party leader Naftali Bennett.

The rally came after years of campaigning by Israeli civil society and opposition parties to establish an independent commission of inquiry on the security failures that led to 7 October.

Netanyahu's government has refused to establish such an independent body, the likes of which Israel has commonly set up in the past to investigate major state-level failings.

It has instead offered to create a "political" commission, half of whose members would be appointed by the ruling coalition and half by opposition lawmakers.

Opposition leaders however said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.

As the campaign draws to an end, Eisenkot and Bennett are expected to hold separate last meetings with voters in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening.

No 'bbCoin'

First-time voter Naama Bitterman, 18, said at Saturday's rally that she was confident the anti-Netanyahu bloc she supports would have the upper hand in the vote and improve Israel's international standing, tarnished by three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and surging violence in the occupied West Bank.

"I think that if we win -- and we are going to win -- we can change how other people in the entire world see us," she told AFP.

Britain and several other countries imposed sanctions targeting goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in response to a wave of settler attacks on Palestinians and settlement construction approved by Netanyahu's right-wing government.

To circumvent Israel's growing international isolation, Netanyahu suggested Friday that Israel may need to develop an alternate digital economy.

Netanyahu, who has previously called for Israel to become self-sufficient militarily, also said that multibillion-dollar weapons packages from key ally Washington "won't keep coming".

Opposition leaders on Saturday lambasted the premier's suggestion.

Eisenkot sarcastically referred to the proposed parallel digital currency as "bbCoin," using a common nickname for the premier, Bibi.

"Netanyahu says that if he is elected again, Israel will disconnect from the global economy. No online shopping, no investments in high-tech, no security. We must not let bbCoin destroy Israel," he wrote on X.

Yair Lapid, a former prime minister and current leader of the opposition, accused Netanyahu of "promising Israeli citizens before the elections that they will stand in line for an hour and a half for bread like in Russia or Iran".

"If he wins the elections, that's what will happen: there will be sanctions, there will be no security agreement with the United States... and there will be no Israeli economy," he said in an interview with Israel's Channel 12.

item.title: Air pollution very high in 9 areas of Dhaka
item.description:
Dhaka ranked fifth among the world’s major cities for air pollution on Sunday morning.

According to the latest ranking published by Swiss-based organisation IQAir at 8:30 am, Dhaka recorded an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 173. Air at this level is considered “unhealthy”.

Air pollution levels were particularly high in nine areas of Dhaka, with one location recording a “very unhealthy” level.

Kuching in Malaysia and Mumbai in India ranked first and second, with scores of 210 and 191 respectively.

The main pollutant in Dhaka’s air was fine particulate matter (PM2.5), with a concentration of 88.5 micrograms per cubic metre. This is approximately 17 times higher than the World Health Organization (WHO)’s annual guideline level. IQAir calculated the figures using data from 12 monitoring stations across Dhaka.

Air pollution raises dengue death risk, fuels diabetes, other chronic diseases

Air pollution levels across Dhaka

Among Dhaka’s monitoring stations, Abdullahbagh in North Badda recorded the highest AQI score, at 201. An AQI score above 200 indicates a “very unhealthy” level of air pollution.

Other areas with high pollution levels in the capital included Gulshan Lake Park (186), the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) office in Agargaon (179), Baridhara Lakeside (179), Baridhara Park Road (177), Becharam Deuri (176), Eastern Housing (173), Grace International School in Gulshan (169) and Base Edge Water in the same area (165).

Dhaka tops global air pollution rankings again: ‘Situation becoming increasingly complex’

Among divisional cities outside Dhaka, Rajshahi recorded the highest level of air pollution, with an AQI score of 169. The scores for other cities were 164 in Khulna, 157 in Rangpur, 155 in Mymensingh, 151 in Barishal, 142 in Chattogram and 112 in Sylhet.

IQAir’s index reflects air quality at a particular moment, so rankings and scores may change over time.

item.title: Prime Minister to visit Japan tomorrow, raising hopes for fresh investment momentum
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will leave for Japan tomorrow, 26 October, on a four-day visit. Alongside a summit meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, he will visit a Toyota factory and a JERA LNG terminal.

During the visit, Japan’s revamped ‘Big-B’ initiative centred on the Bay of Bengal is set to move forward. The updated plan brings investment, energy, maritime security and geopolitics together under a single framework.

Diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Tokyo said the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (Big-B), launched in 2014 at the initiative of then Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, is being updated around four pillars. The revised framework may be reflected in a joint statement following the formal meeting between the two countries’ prime ministers.

At the invitation of Takaichi, Tarique Rahman will visit Japan from 26 to 29 October. During the visit, he will deliver the keynote address at the Japan-Bangladesh Economic Forum and visit an LNG terminal and power plant in Futtsu, Chiba. Bilateral talks with Takaichi are scheduled for 27 October.

Japan has long been one of Bangladesh’s most reliable partners in infrastructure development. Major projects supported by Japan include the Matarbari deep-sea port and power project, the Dhaka Metro Rail and the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.

Diplomatic sources said Tokyo’s role had previously focused largely on loan-based assistance, but the emphasis is now shifting towards commercial partnerships and public-private partnerships (PPPs). The Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) was signed in February this year.

Japan to invest Tk 774.7 billion in Bangladesh

Toyota and JERA: industrialisation and energy

Japanese media outlet Nikkei Asia reported that Japan’s private sector is drawing up plans to invest around one trillion yen in Bangladesh over the next five years, equivalent to approximately Tk 770 billion at current exchange rates.

According to diplomatic sources, a substantial share of the planned investment will go to manufacturing and energy. Japanese automaker Toyota is planning to invest around USD 500 million in an assembly plant in Bangladesh.

People familiar with the matter say that if local suppliers secure contracts to manufacture components and cables, this could help develop a strong network of supporting industries, known as backward linkages. It could also create jobs for young engineers.

Gas shortages in the industrial sector are a major constraint on Bangladesh’s growth. To help address the problem, JERA, Japan’s largest energy producer, has reportedly proposed building an LNG terminal and related infrastructure in the Maheshkhali-Matarbari area.

If implemented, the project could ease pressure on gas and electricity supplies to industry. However, volatility in global energy markets and the cost of the US dollar will remain major challenges.

Diplomatic sources from both countries told this correspondent that Bangladesh is important to Japan as a reliable and economically self-reliant strategic partner in maintaining its position in the Bay of Bengal. Matarbari in Cox’s Bazar lies at the heart of this strategy.

A new version of Big-B: Four pillars

The original Big-B plan in 2014 was largely focused on developing industry and port facilities around Matarbari. Diplomatic sources from both countries said it was now being updated around four pillars in view of the Bay of Bengal’s growing strategic importance.

First, regional connectivity and integrated logistics will be prioritised, with the aim of turning the Matarbari deep-sea port and LNG infrastructure into a hub for international trade. One objective is to facilitate the movement of goods to and from India’s northeastern states, Nepal and Bhutan.

Second, the plan aims to strengthen resilience and geopolitical stability, preparing Bangladesh to serve as an alternative maritime route in the event of natural disasters, global conflicts or supply-chain disruptions.

Third, it seeks to establish modern rules for public-private partnerships and business, reducing bureaucratic obstacles while ensuring internationally recognised, rules-based procedures.

Fourth, it aims to promote regional peace and maritime security by ensuring free and safe navigation in the Bay of Bengal. Japan has already handed over five patrol vessels to the Bangladesh Navy.

A diplomatic source in Tokyo said the visit could also advance arrangements for providing the Coast Guard with a modern 35-metre patrol vessel.

PM’s Japan visit: Reducing metro rail costs, loan interest rates likely to be discussed

Matarbari and Indian Ocean geopolitics

The strategic significance of Big-B lies in the geographical position of the Indian Ocean and the Bay of Bengal. The bay is not only a gateway for Bangladesh’s trade but also a major maritime route connecting South and Southeast Asia.

China is expanding its infrastructure presence and influence in the region through its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). Japan and its allies, meanwhile, have promoted the concept of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP).

Diplomatic sources from both countries told this correspondent that Bangladesh is important to Japan as a reliable and economically self-reliant strategic partner in maintaining its position in the Bay of Bengal. Matarbari in Cox’s Bazar lies at the heart of this strategy.

Once fully operational, the deep-sea port and energy hub could boost not only Bangladesh’s imports and exports but also become an important route for transporting goods to and from northeastern India. This could reshape regional supply chains and create alternative trade routes across South Asia, potentially positioning Bangladesh as a regional logistics hub.

item.title: Houthis say attacked Saudi Arabia, Yemen’s Aden after deadly strikes
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS-SAUDI-AIRPORT

Yemen’s Houthis launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Saturday after blaming the kingdom for strikes that the Iran-backed group said killed 17 people.

Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer, shifting the focus of the wider US-Iran war that erupted in February.

Over the past 24 hours, the Yemeni fighters said they targeted three Saudi airports including the international airport in capital Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.

Military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched missiles at “King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of the Saudi enemy, in two phases”, the airports in Dammam in the east and Najran in the south.

The international airport on Saturday however said it would resume domestic and international flights “effective Sunday” in a post on X, after it was closed following several deadly attacks this month.

The Houthis also launched attacks on the southern Khamis Mushait air base as well as “crude oil pumping stations and the crude oil pipeline from east to west”.

The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles. The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a “huge lie”.

The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.

Authorities said the coast guards headquarters and a second building of theirs as well as Aden airport had been targeted.

The fresh attack claims came after the Houthis’ Al-Masirah TV channel accused the kingdom of separate strikes in Yemen that killed more than a dozen people. Riyadh has not claimed the alleged strikes.

The Houthi broadcaster said a strike on a house in Sanaa killed at least four people, another at a residential building for cement factory workers killed eight and another outside the city of Hodeida killed five from the same family.

Yemen’s civil war, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis against the Saudi-supported and internationally recognised government, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war roiled the region.

Diplomats evacuated

Earlier Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities Taif and Yanbu in the kingdom’s west.

Saudi Arabia’s civil defence had broadcast warnings of “potential danger” for four western regions, including Taif and Yanbu as well as Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest city.

The warning was lifted minutes later.

The group has also targeted the kingdom’s oil infrastructure as well as its airports and tankers.

Yanbu is a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast that has allowed Riyadh to bypass Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz for much of its crude exports via the east-west pipeline.

An attack on Riyadh airport earlier this month killed 13 people and forced it to shut, while this week the US ordered non-essential embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing the Houthi threat.

Riyadh leads a military coalition that first intervened in 2015 in the conflict, which has devastated Yemen and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

The dramatic escalation in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets.

In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.

The Houthis then declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized Yemeni government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.

In response, the Houthis have also reported frequent Saudi strikes targeting areas under their control.

Egypt has suggested sending troops to help defend Saudi Arabia, while Britain and France have offered their forces to protect the Gulf kingdom.

On Saturday the US Mission to the United Arab Emirates and US embassy in Riyadh said Washington’s travel advisories for both Gulf countries were “updated to reflect an increase in potential armed attacks by the Iranian-supported Houthis”.

item.title: Consumers forced to pay more for cooking gas as another price hike looms
item.description:
The shortage of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), used for cooking, shows no sign of easing. Even after the price of the most widely used 12kg cylinder was raised by Tk 252, consumers are still having to pay Tk 500 to Tk 600 above the official price.

In some places, retailers are refusing to take back old cylinders, forcing customers to buy new ones. Meanwhile, the process of raising prices yet again has begun.

The official price of a 12kg LPG cylinder for October has been set at Tk 1,837. However, cylinders are selling for Tk 2,300 to Tk 2,500 in the market. Prices are higher in Dhaka than in districts outside the capital.

Meanwhile, businesses have submitted a proposal for another price hike. The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) will hold a public hearing on the proposal on 29 October.

On Saturday, tea vendor Md Shahed at Karwan Bazar said he had paid Tk 2,500 for a 12kg cylinder. Surma Begum, a resident of Mohammadpur, said she had bought a 12kg cylinder for Tk 2,300 last Friday. However, a relative of hers bought LPG for Tk 2,100 in their village home in Bhola on the same day.

According to sources at the LPG importers’ association, the LPG Operators Association of Bangladesh (LOAB), and the regulatory body BERC, 23 companies in the country have the infrastructure needed to import LPG. Thirteen companies imported LPG in August and 10 in September.

Some companies are buying LPG from others and supplying limited quantities to the market, while others are supplying only nominal amounts. As a result, the supply shortfall persists.

People involved in the LPG sector say prices in the international market rose last month after the war in the Middle East spread to Saudi Arabia. Shipping costs also continued to rise. However, domestic prices were adjusted only on 4 October.

Stockpiling had begun earlier, on 22 September. Importers, distributors and retailers all accumulated stocks, pushing prices up in anticipation of a shortage. Even after BERC raised the official price, the practice of charging consumers more than the fixed rate continued.

International prices have since risen further. Distributors and importers have also demanded increases to cover other costs. Taking their demands into consideration, BERC has scheduled a public hearing for 29 October. There is therefore little prospect of prices falling in the immediate future.

Senior officials of three LPG companies said demand was rising not only for cooking but also in the industrial and transport sectors. They said there would be no shortage if the sector's full storage capacity were used and all cylinders remained in circulation.

Four cylinders are needed to ensure that one LPG cylinder is available to a customer, as the others are required to maintain the supply chain. At present, at least 120,000 tonnes of LPG are supplied each month for cooking.

This enables customers to receive 8.3 million cylinders containing 12kg each. To maintain this supply, 33.2 million cylinders are required, but that number is not regularly available. If at least another six million cylinders were in active circulation, monthly deliveries to customers could increase by 1.5 million cylinders.

BERC Chairman Jalal Ahmed told Prothom Alo that imports had not declined, so there should be no supply crisis. BERC has written to the Energy Division seeking easier letters of credit (LCs) for companies unable to import LPG. The Energy Division has already taken steps, and the situation is improving, he said.

He added that the public hearing would discuss in detail the need to buy different cylinders because of shortages, as well as proposals to raise prices and commissions. The commission will announce its decision after the hearing.

Full capacity not being utilised

According to LOAB and BERC sources, the private sector controls 99 per cent of the LPG market. There are approximately 53 million cylinders in the market. Of these, 30.7 million belong to the 10 companies currently active in the sector. This means 42 per cent of the cylinders are not in regular use.

All companies together have an LPG storage capacity of 180,000 tonnes. The 10 active companies account for 95,000 tonnes of that capacity. In other words, 47 per cent of the sector''s storage capacity remains unused because the other companies are not importing LPG.

As a result, many distributors are unable to obtain LPG and are buying small quantities from other distributors. Consumers are struggling not only with higher prices but also with access to cylinders.

Retailers are unwilling to accept cylinders belonging to companies that have ceased operations. This is forcing some customers to purchase new cylinders. Under the rules, however, all companies are required to take back cylinders, regardless of the brand. The shortage could ease if companies still operating regularly increased cylinder production.

Selim Khan, president of the LPG Business Welfare Association, told Prothom Alo that stockpiling was one problem, but an even bigger issue was that nearly 25 million cylinders were lying idle.

Ten to 12 companies were no longer supplying LPG, he said, leaving many distributors on the verge of bankruptcy and causing hardship for consumers. Measures should be taken to bring these cylinders back into use.

People familiar with the sector say imports have not increased in line with steadily rising demand. At one point, the country imported and supplied 180,000 tonnes of LPG a month. Now, imports do not exceed 160,000 tonnes. Some consumers have turned to alternative cooking fuels, such as electric stoves, to avoid the shortage. Otherwise, the crisis would have been even worse.

Abu Sayeed Raja, chief marketing officer of Fresh LP Gas, told Prothom Alo that the shortage would ease soon and that much of it had already subsided. There would be no supply shortage next month, he said, adding that efforts were under way to increase imports further.

Companies that have suspended imports say some of them have been unable to open LCs for the past two years. Banks are refusing to issue LCs unless the companies deposit the full amount in cash. Frozen bank accounts have also created difficulties with transactions. As a result, they have halted imports.

Regular importers, however, say there are currently no government restrictions. They argue that banks will inevitably create difficulties for companies with large outstanding liabilities, noting that these companies have borrowed thousands of crores of taka and are now unable to import LPG.

The country imported 158,000 tonnes of LPG in August and 156,000 tonnes in September.

Proposal to raise prices

Amirul Haque, president of LOAB, told Prothom Alo that importers were making every possible effort to increase imports and maintain supplies. However, stabilising the market would remain difficult until the situation in the Middle East returned to normal. Government monitoring must continue at every stage of the supply chain to keep the market under control, he said.

On 6 October, BERC sent a letter to the LPG Business Welfare Association regarding the sale of LPG at prices above the official rate.

The association says it is being forced to buy LPG at higher prices. In addition, rising fuel prices, licence fees and other associated costs have made it impossible to sell LPG at the fixed rate. It has demanded an increase in the commission paid on each cylinder. Under its proposal, the commission should rise by Tk 80 per cylinder. Retailers'' commissions may also increase.

Importing companies, known as operators, have also proposed a price hike. They say BERC sets the monthly price based on Saudi Aramco''s contract price, the premium covering shipping and insurance, the exchange rate of the US dollar and fuel prices. However, other costs have also risen over the past five years, and prices must therefore be increased, they argue.

M Shamsul Alam, energy adviser to the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), told Prothom Alo that several companies had stockpiled LPG to create an artificial shortage. They had extracted more than Tk 6 billion in additional revenue in a single month, he alleged.

Now, another hearing is being held to raise prices further. Consumers are being held hostage in what he described as a market driven by profiteering, while BERC remains inactive.

He called for a judicial investigation to identify and punish those involved in stockpiling, adding that their licences should be cancelled if necessary.

item.title: Sajek incident not the problem, but symptom of deeper problem
item.description:
It is not appropriate to view the incidents happening over the past few days in Sajek, Rangamati as isolated events. Seeing them as isolated might make some believe it's a significant law and order problem affecting the burgeoning tourism industry in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Many might think deploying more law enforcement agencies is required to address this issue. However, understanding the underlying problem that these incidents are merely symptoms of a long-standing issue in the Chittagong Hill Tracts will be challenging without a proper diagnosis and treatment.

What is the core issue of the Chittagong Hill Tracts? Since the 1980s, several dialogues have occurred between the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti (PCJSS) and the governments of the Jatiya Party, BNP, and Awami League. The Chittagong Hill Tracts issue has been identified in dialogues as a political problem. The people of different ethnic groups in this region demand self-governance, land ownership security, and constitutional recognition of their identities. They have enjoyed these rights since the Mughal, British, and Pakistani times. Even after the independence of Bangladesh, they have been pressing their demands. These demands could be politically fulfilled. For political fulfillment, the Chittagong Hill Tracts Agreement was signed between the government and the PCJSS on 2 December 1997, which is widely known as the Peace Accord both locally and internationally.

Recent incidents in Sajek can be seen as a reflection of the despair of the local populace. Whether the road blockade and subsequent events over dominance by two regional organisations in the Machalong and Baghaighat areas of Sajek are logical or illogical; incidents are occurring nonetheless. Nearly three thousand tourists were trapped in panic, disrupting the normal life of local people.

But in the 29 years since then, has the Peace Accord of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, which held many hopes and aspirations for the hill residents, been implemented? According to the PCJSS, as part of preparing for the implementation of the 1997 agreement, various agencies like the Ministry of Chittagong Hill Tracts, District and Regional Councils, Land Dispute Resolution Commission, and Refugee Rehabilitation Task Force were formed. However, the implementation remains stagnant as of 1998. Key aspects such as law and order maintenance, district police, and land management have not been implemented. In some cases, there have been efforts to implement certain aspects, while at the same time, there has been counteraction to impede these efforts.

Initially, for the implementation of the agreement, transferring the police department to the district council to maintain law and order (as mentioned in Article 24 of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Agreement, which states that, regardless of other laws, all personnel from sub-inspector to lower levels in the hill district police will be appointed under council supervision in the prescribed manner) was crucial. Because maintaining law and order during the agreement period was a prerequisite for its implementation. Yet, no steps have been taken in these 29 years to transfer the police department.

If it had, personnel could have been appointed based on community-based seats in the district council. Consequently, controlling law and order would have been easier with a mixed police force comprising people from various communities like Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Mro, Bom, Khiyang, and Khumi.
Language remains a significant barrier in working in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. There are 12 languages from 12 ethnic groups, including Chakma, Marma, and Bengalis. One ethnic group's language is not understood by another.

Mutual trust and belief, which are essential for security arrangements and law and order improvement, can be achieved through language. If members of various ethnic groups and languages were in the mixed police force, the language barrier with local language speakers could be eliminated. The police would become a multi-ethnic force. Currently, almost all members of the police and other law enforcement agencies deployed in the hill region are Bengali. They do not understand the language of any hill ethnic groups, have no clear concept about the local culture, and are unfamiliar with the geographical positioning.

In such circumstances, despite being amidst thousands of people, they can't comprehend the current environment and situation. On the other hand, due to linguistic isolation, local inhabitants cannot place their trust in them. Such mutual distrust becomes a significant obstacle to maintaining and improving law and order.

Yet, for implementing the Chittagong Hill Tracts Agreement, mutual trust, improvement, and stability in law and order are crucial. The agreement implementation remains elusive for nearly three decades due to non-fulfillment of these conditions. Here, the laxity of government sincerity mainly comes into question.

Before the agreement, during almost two and a half decades of unrest, the people of this region had suffered physical, mental, and various forms of harassment. According to the Task Force on Refugee and Internally Displaced Persons Rehabilitation, nearly 90,000 families of different ethnic groups in the three hill districts became internally displaced, losing their homes. At that time, almost two-thirds of people were from hill ethnic groups.

Nearly 70,000 took refuge in India and returned as refugees. These harassed people were overwhelmingly hopeful with the Peace Accord of 1997. Those who didn't witness this would need help understanding. However, when they later saw the agreement not being implemented, much like prior to the agreement, with new symptoms and various factions and sub-factions emerging, their exuberant hope transformed into despair over an uncertain future.

Recent incidents in Sajek can be seen as a reflection of the despair of the local populace. Whether the road blockade and subsequent events over dominance by two regional organisations in the Machalong and Baghaighat areas of Sajek are logical or illogical; incidents are occurring nonetheless. Nearly three thousand tourists were trapped in panic, disrupting the normal life of local people. This situation clearly shows that government initiatives to implement the Chittagong Hill Tracts Agreement and resolve the region’s issues are necessary. Without a reasonable and acceptable solution, the recurrence of incidents like Sajek will continue.

item.title: Clashes break out in Paris, other French cities amid fresh protests
item.description:
Clashes broke out Saturday in Paris and other French cities amid demonstrations held a week after others that degenerated into street violence and prompted a robust security backlash as President Emmanuel Macron seeks to restore order.
Police arrested nearly 1,000 people as officers were confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from black-clad "ultra-left" extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
Riot police squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes.
Two people were "seriously" injured, Nunez said: one man in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.
Authorities had deployed 70,000 security forces across the country for the new marches, called to protest the cost of living.
The violence came a week after rioting that saw public buildings vandalised, hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people arrested, casting a pall over a country that goes to the polls in six months to choose a successor to Macron after 10 years.
Nunez said Saturday's outcome was more "positive" than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses.
There was nevertheless widespread anger at the government over a protest crackdown viewed as an assault on the right to protest.
Saturday's demonstrations drew between 410,000 and 800,000 people across the country, according to different estimates by authorities and the organising CGT union.
The main Paris march had between 110,000 and 250,000 attendees, according to those sources.
Macron's government has ordered police to prevent protesters reaching city centres, where shops are concentrated, and in Paris and some other cities, partial curfews were imposed in certain urban zones. The French president had ordered non-union demonstrations be banned as "illegitimate".
In Paris, where many shops had boarded up windows to prevent looting, and the Louvre and the Musee d'Orsay museums shut for the day, the main demonstration passed off largely peacefully.
The march had been pushed to the capital's southeast rim under a last-minute order by authorities.
Afterwards, though, clashes broke out as the crowd was dispersing. Nunez said the confrontations lasted two hours and involved "500 rioters" at the back of the march.
AFP journalists saw police charge several times and vigorously use tear gas and batons against some, mostly young, protesters.
"The police started moving towards everyone, telling them to get down and back off. They were just taking people down, you know, beating protesters," one demonstrator bleeding from a baton blow to his face, who gave his first name as David, told AFP.
In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through lines of police firing tear gas and a water cannon to reach the city centre, an AFP journalist there witnessed.
Emma, 23, marching in the northwest city of Rennes, said she was angry at "everything happening at the moment", denouncing the bans on demonstrations and the "repression" of the high schools student protests.
Marching in the rain at the head of the protest in the northern city of Lille, 47-year-old Delphine insisted: "Neither the president, nor the weather will stop me from demonstrating."
In Lyon, police used tear gas to disperse around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city.
"If they prohibit protests then that means we are heading more and more towards a regime that is fascist, that is dictatorial," said one 20-year-old protester in Lyon, who gave only his first name, Silem.
In the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, far-right activists came out onto the streets seeking confrontations with "ultra-left militants", in what authorities said was an unprecedented development.
There was looting on the sidelines of the marches in Marseille and Grenoble, said police.
Meanwhile, the Yellow Vests, who staged disruptive protests against Macron eight years ago, called for more demonstrations on October 31 for "the freedom to protest".
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who marched in the Paris rally, said Macron "is going to understand that this is going to repeat itself every week".
Tensions were heightened by a rally in the city of Orleans by far-right leader Marine Le Pen's National Rally party to kick off her campaign for the presidential election.
Thousands of counter-protesters chanting anti-fascist slogans marched in the city. Police put their number at 13,000 while organisers said twice as many participated.
The unrest across France highlighted the febrile political atmosphere ahead of the vote, in which Le Pen leads in surveys.
Inflation in France, particularly affecting the cost of fuel, has surged since the start of the Middle East war in February.
Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has mobilised 500 troops to Milan after street violence there.

item.title: Logistical deficits not a good enough excuse for law enforcement
item.description:
There is no denying the grueling realities faced by ground-level law enforcement personnel in Bangladesh.
It cannot be easy to operate amid severe logistical deficits, including acute transport shortages and a lack of proper housing facilities, for nearly 90% of the force. Officers also often endure grueling 12-to-16-hour shifts under immense pressure.
This is a reality we must acknowledge, and we sympathize with those within the forces.
Equipping the force with necessary transport, housing, and operational backing is thus a vital administrative duty that the government must address without delay.
However, recognizing the genuine hardships of police work must never translate into a blanket excuse for systemic failure or poor public service.
The primary grievance of ordinary citizens with law enforcement agencies has been an entrenched culture of authoritarian intimidation and a callous disregard for public welfare.
Too often, the badge has been wielded as an instrument of power and coercion rather than protection, leaving communities alienated and terrified of the very institutions meant to secure them.
Logistical upgrades and multi-crore vehicle procurements will mean nothing if the internal ethos of the force remains rot-ridden.
A lack of transport does not excuse extortion at checkpoints, nor does substandard housing justify custodial abuse, bribery, or the routine weaponization of the law against the vulnerable.
For generations, citizens have been forced to navigate a police apparatus that views them with suspicion or contempt rather than dignity and service. For that to change, it will take more than overhauling institutional capacity.
Accountability must match investment step for step. Officers deserve fair working conditions and adequate resources, but the public deserves law enforcement agencies that genuinely care for and protect them.

item.title: Where is the justice?
item.description:
There's an old saying that all of economics is either footnotes to Adam Smith or wrong.
Like most old sayings, it's not wholly and exactly correct but there is still a great deal of truth in it.
For one of the reasons that old sayings survive is that people note there's a lot of truth in there and so keep repeating it.
That we've still got the saying can thus be a proof that there's a useful amount of truth in it.
With that in mind, we can discuss the disaster that is this news : “Bangladesh ranked 123rd among 143 countries and jurisdictions in the World Justice Project (WJP) index” and justice here is referring to things like corruption, regulatory enforcement, and so on, eight areas in total.
The one that concerns us here is “civil justice was the second-weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 132nd and scoring 0.36.”
We know about corruption, about the ineffectiveness of regulatory enforcement, and so on. But thieves and incompetence we also don't want. The effectiveness -- or not -- of civil justice is one of those things not enough people think about enough of the time.
Adam Smith did point out that “little else is requisite to carry a state to the highest degree of opulence from the lowest barbarism but peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice: All the rest being brought about by the natural course of things.”
Peace we're all doing pretty well on in this corner of the world. Easy taxes could be easier but the Bangladeshi state does not swallow an inordinate amount of everyone's production or work.
Which leaves us that administration of justice.
Given that we are talking about the economy here, it's that part of justice associated with the economy that matters to us.
The ability to go to court and get as the contract enforced -- say. Which is, as we know, a wholly laughable proposition in the Bangladeshi courts of today. Which is, therefore, the thing that needs to be fixed.
We can also borrow something from our other ideas about the economy. That, in business at least, it is often better to make a fast decision than delay and then, perhaps, make the right one.
Borrowing that idea means that the law, about contracts and commerce, needs to be fast. It's better that it be fast than it be wholly just or near perfect.
A decision -- even, sometimes the wrong one -- given now is better than grinding through the process for another five years.
Something that will be anathema to the lawyers of course, they get paid by the hour, but still true all the same.
It would be even better if we always got the right decisions -- but let's do this step by step. We need commercial law -- that part of civil justice which works with business and the economy -- to be swift.
We also need it to be certain. If the contract says something, it must be definitive. The same is true for the law -- that's what the decision will be.
Those decisions need to come quickly. These two conditions are more important than grinding through to a decision in a decade.
It's not wholly true that Adam Smith was correct about everything he discussed but it's still a remarkably good basis to start our reasoning from. As he points out, there are things that governments really do have to do in order to ensure that the economy grows.
One of these is a commercial legal system that actually works. And by works, we mean swift and certain decisions more than necessarily wholly fair or even correct ones.
As the World Justice Project's index points out, this is something Bangladesh is failing upon and failing badly. We should correct that error.
We all know that it's going to take years, if not decades, to recover the money from those who looted the banks last decade. If nothing else about efficient justice, it would be nice to bankrupt the thieves before they die, no? You know, the tolerable administration of justice.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Weaponizing humiliation
item.description:
Perhaps there is no such thing as privacy in Bangladesh. Even where it exists, many in the authorities or the media do not understand what it means. Even if they do understand, they are unwilling to act according to the essence of privacy.
This unwillingness is strongest when an opportunity arises to violate a woman’s privacy. Society has still not found any way to suppress the urge to humiliate women in public.
Last Tuesday, personnel of the detective branch raided the residence of an Additional DIG of police in Purbachal, near Dhaka. It was described as an anti-narcotics operation (though these days even a raid on a club or bar is called an “anti-narcotics operation”). But there did not seem to be much presence of drugs there.
In the photos released, although there was a bottle and a half of liquor, the absence of narcotics was noticeable. However, that is not the problem with this operation. The question is about the way the operation was publicized in the media, or the way arrangements were made to publicize it.
Some days ago, during a police raid on a club called German Club in Dhaka, the entire scene was being filmed from outside the main gate. As the club’s guests came out one by one, they were filmed, and the video was spread on social media, with one particular woman going viral on social media.
But what happened in Purbachal was even more disgraceful, and here it was not only the unbridled content creators of social media, but even established mainstream news media that got involved.
Videos were shot inside the Purbachal house, in various rooms. When several girls came down the stairs from the upper floor, one or two tried to cover their faces with their orna (scarf) while their faces were being filmed, but most could not.
The men present also appeared in the video, though the focus was mostly on the women. Hearing the description of the raid, many will assume that some “immoral activity” was going on there. And when, on top of that, one woman’s face after another appears in the video, no psychologist is needed to understand what picture forms in the public’s mind.
Here the question may be asked: Which is the immoral activity? Adult men and women socializing inside a home? Or is it the filming of women, calling the house a “harem,” and humiliating them socially?
By shooting and circulating the video, the women were not merely humiliated. They were humiliated knowingly and deliberately, and their safety was put at risk.
One thing needs to be made clear. It is normal for police to record videos in any operation. It is important to preserve through video information such as whether the operation is being conducted according to the police’s own rules, how and where evidence was found, and how and where the detainees were held.
But that video would be the police’s own evidence, meant to assist their own investigation, an important part of the process of collecting testimony and evidence against the accused.
Such a video will play an important role in framing formal charges and conducting the case. Similarly, the accused’s lawyers can use these same police videos to try to get the allegations against their client dismissed. But the videos of the recent operations do not seem to have been taken to assist a case.
First, it is not clear who shot the videos. At least from the video taken outside the gate of German Club, it seemed that it was no one from the police. That is, someone who got news of the raid went there and filmed it.
Is the Purbachal incident the same? The videos were taken both inside and outside the house. One woman was seen pointing a finger at the person filming and saying something. Had someone from the police been holding the camera, that woman would perhaps not have done so.
The most disgraceful thing was spreading those videos on social media, exposing the women’s faces, and humiliating them in public.
Such an incident, while not common, once again begs the question of ethics in a section of the country’s media. Law enforcement agencies also have a big role in building this habit.
For many years, the police, and later RAB or BGB, have been supplying the media with photos and identities of people detained on charges of some alleged crime.
Even when the detainee was only a suspect, his photo was given to the media, often with a signboard calling him a criminal hung around his neck. This still happens.
That a person is innocent until proven guilty in court, this fundamental principle of law seems to be unknown to Bangladesh’s law enforcement agencies.
The Bangladeshi media industry too has never quite had anything in the way of editorial policy or ethical standards. Some large organizations have discussed ethics and, in some cases, tried to create a policy of their own.
For example, at one time the photos and identities of women who were victims of rape used to be printed. But that has changed. The identity of victims is now kept secret in most cases.
But the accused also deserve this kind of protection. Formal charges can be framed against someone only when there is sufficient evidence, and until charges are framed, the identity of the accused should also be kept secret.
Even now, photos of accused or suspected persons provided by the police are being published along with their identities. As for social media content creators, that is a separate matter, and it is doubtful whether there is any editorial vetting in their work.
In many cases, such creators run a channel single-handedly, and they depend entirely on view counts and engagement for income. They do not have time to worry about editorial “decency” or ethical considerations.
Established mainstream media is a different matter. They have staff and the capacity to read and think about what has been done in other countries of the world on journalistic rules, editorial policy, ethics, and so on.
It is possible for them to create their own policies on how to report while protecting the rights, privacy, and safety of ordinary people, and to give journalists the necessary training on these matters.
In particular, established media can sensitize journalists on how to cover delicate stories involving women, children, religious or ethnic minorities, and other vulnerable groups.
This work should have been done long ago. But even now, photos, names, and identities of detainees provided by the police are still being published.
The media needs to think about how their reporting can harm ordinary people. Care must be taken so that people who are innocent in the eyes of the law are not declared “guilty” in a media trial and socially humiliated.
Humiliating those who have no power, who are not wealthy, who have no connections in high circles, and who have no influential mama-chacha in political circles is not merely wrong. It is quite literally another crime. This is especially so when women’s photos or videos are being published with no regard for their social dignity and safety.
Just as initiative is needed from the media industry to stop this practice, the government also needs to impose restrictions on the police so that they do not do anything that could humiliate people before a trial in court.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Nothing is more important than protecting our children
item.description:
The recurring reports of physical and sexual abuse of children within educational institutions across the country lay bare what can only be termed a horrifying national failure.
When schools, madrasas, and learning centres - places meant to nurture and protect our nation’s youth - become sites of predatory violence and terror, the foundational contract between society and the state is shattered.
Recent alarms raised by child rights advocates regarding abuse cases expose a pervasive, systemic rot that can no longer be ignored or swept under the rug with bureaucratic platitudes.
For too long, child protection in Bangladesh has been undermined by a culture of silence, social stigma, and institutional cover-ups. Predators are allowed to operate with virtual impunity, exploiting power imbalances to silence vulnerable victims through threats and intimidation.
When children are forced to choose between their education and their personal safety, the institutional framework entrusted with their welfare has utterly collapsed.
Protecting children cannot remain a rhetorical talking point for NGOs and press releases. The government must immediately enforce rigorous, binding child-protection protocols across every educational institution nationwide, without exception.
Allegations of abuse must be met with swift, impartial criminal investigation, prosecution, and absolute accountability, stripping away the impunity enjoyed by so many perpetrators.
Educational authorities too must do their part by establishing secure, confidential reporting channels and robust psychosocial support systems, ensuring that victims and their families are believed, protected, and prioritized.
A nation that fails to safeguard its children from predators within its own classrooms has forfeited its moral authority. We need to be getting rid of this rot with the urgency it warrants, ruthlessly purging abusive environments and transforming our schools and madrasas into genuine safe havens before more generations of children are scarred by institutional cowardice.

item.title: Dhaka ranks world's third most polluted city Sunday morning
item.description:
Dhaka ranked as the world's third most polluted city on Sunday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 176 at 10:30am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy" category, indicating that the concentration of airborne pollutants had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general public, according to the AQI scale.
Pakistan’s Lahore topped the list with an AQI score of 207, followed by Malaysia’s Kuching at 203, while India’s Mumbai ranked fourth with a score of 173.
An AQI reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while a score between 151 and 200 is classified as "unhealthy". Readings between 201 and 300 are deemed "very unhealthy", and levels above 301 are considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI, an index that tracks daily air quality, indicates how polluted the air is and the potential health effects on residents.
In Bangladesh, AQI measurements are based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and ozone.
According to the World Health Organization, air pollution causes an estimated seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Over 6,000 cases pending with Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunals in Rangpur
item.description:
More than 6,000 cases remain pending with three Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunals in Rangpur, with over 300 rape and dowry cases awaiting trial for five to 18 years, leaving victims and accused trapped in prolonged legal battles.
Over 2,000 of the pending cases involve rape, while victims say repeated court appearances and mounting legal expenses have pushed many families into financial hardship.
A visit to the tribunals revealed the plight of litigants who have spent years seeking justice. Sharifa Yasmin, from Anandanagar village in Pirgachha upazila, said her husband and in-laws drove her out of their home because she could not pay Tk200,000 in dowry.
She filed a case six years ago, but the trial has yet to begin. With hearings scheduled roughly every two months, Sharifa said she had sold cattle, goats, ducks and chickens to cover travel costs and court-related expenses.
Other women, including Asma Begum of Pirgachha and Mariam Begum of Rangpur Sadar, also described similar experiences.
Asma, a poor woman, said her daughter was abducted and raped eight years ago, but the trial had yet to begin.
Sohrab Hossain of Bhandarbari village in Pirgachha said he had been attending court for 18 years in connection with a rape case filed against him. Working as a rickshaw puller in Dhaka, he returns to Rangpur every two months for hearings.
He said he could not afford to miss a hearing for fear of an arrest warrant, forcing him to spend money on repeated journeys while struggling to earn a living.
Human rights activists and legal experts blamed the delays on a shortage of judges, police failures to produce witnesses and a lack of diligence by those involved in prosecution.
Rumana Zaman, president of Rangpur district chapter of Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, said the law sets time limits for disposing of cases involving violence against women and children, yet many litigants spend years waiting for justice. She called for more judges to expedite trials.
Rights activist Monowara Begum warned that the failure to punish offenders was allowing violence, rape and dowry-related abuse to persist. She also urged authorities to increase the number of judges and ensure speedy trials.
Shafi Kamal, special public prosecutor at Tribunal-1, said nearly 2,000 cases were awaiting trial at his court. He cited the absence of complainants and witnesses on scheduled dates, along with other procedural complications, as reasons for the growing backlog. He said judges and prosecutors were working to ensure justice for litigants.
Moksedul Haque, special public prosecutor at Tribunal-2, said they were also trying to expedite proceedings.
Legal experts called for a dedicated cell to speed up the disposal of cases involving violence against women and children in Rangpur, alongside stricter monitoring by the High Court.
